query: The Co-free FeNiCrMn system was selected to reduce cost while retaining the mechanical performance of equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi; prior work reported comparable or better mechanical properties after excluding Co. Research on FeNiCrMn has mainly addressed corrosion, while studies of related high- and medium-entropy alloys examined dynamic responses under tension or compression, different temperatures and strain rates, compositional changes, and the presence of cracks or voids. Those studies established that dynamic properties are sensitive to loading regime and material condition, but their different chemistries and defect states do not identify what governs FeNiCrMn. Under the constraints of retaining the Co-free composition and its strength–ductility balance, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis explains the dynamic behavior of solidified FeNiCrMn across temperature and strain-rate regimes? Define a controlled study capable of testing the hypothesis, its applicable boundaries, the prior findings that support it, and a result that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In as‐solidified Co‐free equiatomic FeNiCrMn, the dynamic mechanical behavior across temperature and strain-rate regimes is governed by a transition between temperature‐activated dislocation mobility and the onset of deformation twinning. At higher temperatures and lower strain rates, enhanced dislocation glide dominates, while at lower temperatures and higher strain rates, limited thermal activation promotes deformation twinning that contributes to the strength–ductility balance.
generation.intervention: Perform systematic dynamic tensile and/or compressive tests over a matrix of temperatures (cryogenic to elevated) and strain rates (low to high) while maintaining the as‐solidified state, followed by microstructural characterization via transmission electron microscopy (TEM) to assess dislocation structures and twin formation.
generation.conditions: Tests performed on as‐solidified samples without further thermomechanical processing, spanning a broad temperature range and various strain rates to distinctly capture regimes where dislocation glide or twinning would be expected.
generation.structural_mediator: Quantitative changes in dislocation density and twin boundaries
generation.mechanism: At high temperatures and low strain rates, thermal activation promotes dislocation glide and recovery, leading to deformation dominated by dislocation motion. In contrast, at cryogenic temperatures and/or high strain rates, reduced dislocation mobility forces the alloy to accommodate deformation via twinning, aiding in the preservation of ductility despite increased strength.
generation.predicted_outcome: Mechanical tests will reveal that at elevated temperatures and lower strain rates, the material displays typical flow behavior with lower yield strength and minimal twinning, whereas at lower temperatures and higher strain rates, increased yield strength and strain hardening coupled with a higher density of deformation twins will emerge, correlating with shifts in the stress‐strain response.
generation.baseline: Static or moderate rate tests at room temperature where dislocation glide primarily governs deformation with relatively few twins observed.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis is applicable to as‐solidified, Co‐free FeNiCrMn alloys without additional alloying elements or processing that might introduce nano-precipitates or altered defect states. It may not hold if significant post-solidification processing fundamentally changes the microstructural features.
generation.uncertainty: The precise temperature and strain rate thresholds at which the transition between dislocation mobility and twinning occurs remain to be quantified, and other microstructural factors (e.g., grain size or short-range order) might modify the predicted behavior.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare as‐solidified FeNiCrMn samples and conduct a matrix of dynamic mechanical tests varying both temperature (e.g., cryogenic, room temperature, and elevated) and strain rate. Post-test, use TEM and electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD) to quantify dislocation densities and twin fractions.
measurements: Stress–strain curves to assess yield strength, ductility, and strain hardening behavior
TEM/EBSD analyses to quantify dislocation density
Quantitative assessment of twin boundary density and volume fraction
Correlation of mechanical response with observed microstructural changes
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If across the tested conditions no systematic increase in twin formation is observed under low temperature and high strain rate conditions relative to high temperature/low strain rate conditions, or if the dominant deformation mechanism remains unchanged despite variations in test parameters, then the hypothesis will be considered falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Abstract The microstructure, temperature-dependent mechanical properties and deformation behaviors of equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi high-entropy alloy (HEA) additively manufactured by selective laser melting (SLM) were investigated. SLM-built HEA had a face-centered cubic (FCC) single-phase random solid solution. In addition, SLM-built HEA was composed of epitaxial growth grains, dislocation network and nano-sized oxides. Room- and high-temperature compression tests confirmed that SLM-built HEA has outstanding mechanical properties in all temperature ranges compared to equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi HEAs reported up to the present. The excellent mechanical properties of SLM-built HEA were achieved with fine grains, high dislocation density and fine precipitates at low temperatures (25 °C to 600 °C), and by high dislocation density and fine precipitates at high temperatures (700 °C or higher). On the other hand, the deformation microstructure showed that slip and deformation twins are the main deformation mechanisms from 25 °C to 600 °C, and slip and partial recrystallization are the main deformation mechanisms above 700 °C. High-entropy alloys (HEAs), as a novel type of material generally consisting of five or more principle elements, have attracted extensive attention in recent years because of their attractive crystallographic and mechanical properties [ [1] , [2] , [3] , [4] , [5] , [6] , [7] ]. Although it is anticipated that simple solid solution phases are easier to form rather than the intermetallic compounds or complex-ordered phases due to their high configurational entropy [ [8] , [9] ], only a few HEAs have exactly single and stable solid solution structures, among which CoCrFeNiMn alloy is widely concerned [ [10] , [11] , [12] , [13] , [14] ]. It possesses a single face-center-cubic (fcc) solid solution phase even after a series of thermomechanical processing [ [15] , [16] ] and its constituent elements have more sluggish diffusion compared to other conventional alloys [ [17] ]. These characterizations contribute to excellent mechanical properties with a satisfactory combination between tensile strength and ductility [ [18] , [19] ]. decision.trend: Early HEA studies established baseline mechanical properties (strength, ductility) in as‐solidified or cast alloys, but later work—especially on alloys like CoCrFeMnNi—began probing dynamic behavior under variable temperatures and strain rates. These studies showed that the deformation mode (e.g., dislocation glide, twinning, or possible phase transformations) changes with loading rate and thermal activation. However, FeNiCrMn has not been directly examined under dynamic conditions; its static properties were inferred from corrosion-focused work while related alloys provided hints that microstructural mechanisms (such as dislocation pinning by short-range order or the onset of twinning) may govern strain-rate sensitivity and temperature dependence.
decision.unsolved: It remains unresolved which single mechanistic factor governs the dynamic response of Co‐free, as‐solidified FeNiCrMn across a wide range of temperatures and strain rates while retaining the inherent strength–ductility balance. Specifically, the roles of temperature‐activated dislocation mobility versus the onset of twinning or other deformation modes in this Co‐free system have not been isolated.
decision.lever: Perform systematic dynamic mechanical tests (tensile and/or compressive) on as‐solidified FeNiCrMn, varying temperature (from cryogenic to elevated) and strain rate, coupled with microstructural characterization (e.g., TEM analysis of dislocations and twins)
decision.why: This approach directly builds on the trend seen in related HEA studies, isolating the effects of strain rate and temperature on deformation modes. It tests the hypothesis that the dynamic behavior of FeNiCrMn is governed by the interplay between dislocation mobility and the activation of twin formation (or similar deformation mechanisms) under distinct thermal and strain-rate regimes. A lack of transition in deformation mode or a mismatch between the microstructurally observed mechanisms and the bulk mechanical behavior would falsify the hypothesis.
